patients.summary: Elementary school teacher with Addison disease who joins in 2022; Hashimoto hypothyroidism completes autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome type 2, then celiac disease, vitiligo, rheumatoid arthritis and alopecia areata follow. In 2025 she converts to Graves disease, has thyroid storm and a thyroidectomy, and in July 2026 an adrenal crisis on the morning of a planned cholecystectomy.

documents.author: front desk
documents.body: Caller would like to transfer her primary care here; her old office is dropping her plan's network for membership and she'd rather have a doctor she can text. Teacher, so wants a summer slot. Booked new patient visit 8/16 at 9:00. Membership packet emailed. Records release sent for her prior primary-care office and she says her adrenal doctor is with an outside endocrinology group, she'll bring her med bottles.

procedures.procedure: Office visit, new patient, moderate MDM

documents.title: New Patient Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
32F teacher transferring care.

Adrenal: primary adrenal insufficiency diagnosed in her mid-20s (per pt; records requested). Managed by an outside endocrinology group, seen about yearly. On hydrocortisone 20 mg on waking and 10 mg around 4 pm, fludrocortisone 0.1 mg daily. Knows to double hydrocortisone with fever; has never needed the ED for it.

Other hx: iron deficiency anemia some years ago, took ferrous sulfate for several months at the old office, finished, no repeat that she knows of. No surgeries. No hospitalizations.

Meds as above. NKDA.

Family: mother has type 1 diabetes and Hashimoto. Sister with vitiligo. Maternal aunt also has adrenal insufficiency.

Social: married, teaches second grade. Never smoked, doesn't drink. Walks most evenings.

ROS: energy so-so by late afternoon, which she puts down to the job. Otherwise negative.

Exam: well appearing. Vitals as charted, BMI ~24. Skin normal color, no hyperpigmentation of creases or gums. Thyroid not enlarged to my exam. Heart RRR, lungs clear, abdomen soft. No edema.

A/P
1. Primary adrenal insufficiency - stable on current replacement. CMP today for Na/K. Continue meds; refills here are fine, endo sets doses. Asked her to keep her endo visits.
2. Hx iron deficiency anemia - CBC today.
3. Health maintenance - Pap with HPV collected today. HIV and hep C screen once. Tdap given (last one she can't recall). Flu/COVID at a fall nurse visit.
Return for physical next summer or sooner as needed.

documents.title: Results from your visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Hi Riley - your sodium and potassium look right where they should on your fludrocortisone, kidney and liver numbers are normal, and your blood count is normal with no sign of the old anemia. HIV and hepatitis C screens were negative. The Pap and HPV test were both normal, so that's done for five years. Talk soon.

documents.title: Records from prior primary care office
documents.author: medical records
documents.body:
42 pages received by fax from the patient's previous primary-care office, covering about six years. Summary for the chart:
- Primary adrenal insufficiency on hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone, managed by outside endocrinology; copies of two endocrine letters, both stable.
- Iron deficiency anemia on an older CBC, treated with oral iron; follow-up CBC normal.
- Annual exams with normal BMPs and CBCs. Prior cervical cytology normal.
- Allergies: none known.
Filed to media. Nothing outstanding.

documents.title: Immunization visit
documents.author: RN
documents.body: In after school for flu (L deltoid) and bivalent COVID booster (R deltoid). Reviewed: she knows to take her stress dose of hydrocortisone if she runs a fever afterward. Waited 15 min, no reaction.

procedures.procedure: Office visit, established patient, moderate MDM

documents.title: Office Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
S: Tired for most of the past year even with 8 hours of sleep; she had chalked it up to work but it's worse this fall. Hair feels coarse and is breaking. Husband says her eyes look puffy in the mornings. Constipated more days than not. No fever, no neck pain, has not lost weight. Taking hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone every day, no missed doses, no salt craving or dizziness.

O: Vitals as charted. Skin dry, a little cool. Thyroid feels diffusely enlarged and firm, no discrete nodule, not tender. Heart regular. Reflexes slow to relax at the ankles.

A/P: Fatigue with dry skin, hair change and a goiter. With her Addison disease and her mother's Hashimoto, autoimmune hypothyroidism is first on the list. TSH, free T4 today; BMP and CBC to make sure the adrenal side and the old anemia aren't part of it. Will message results. If the thyroid is off I'll ask her endocrinologist to see her sooner rather than at her spring visit.

orders.reason: TSH 16.8, free T4 0.5, goiter; known Addison disease

documents.title: Thyroid results
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Riley, your thyroid is underactive: TSH 16.8 (high) and free T4 0.5 (low). That fits how you've been feeling. Electrolytes and blood count were fine. I've sent a referral and called your endocrinology office; they can see you on the 21st instead of March. Because thyroid and adrenal treatment interact, I'd like them to start the thyroid medicine. Hang in there.

documents.title: RE: Thyroid results
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Thank you!! honestly relieved there's a reason. I'll be there on the 21st.

conditions.label: Autoimmune polyglandular failure
conditions.note: Autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome type 2: Addison disease with Hashimoto thyroiditis.

medications.sig: Take 1 tablet by mouth daily on an empty stomach

documents.title: Endocrinology consultation
documents.author: endocrinology
documents.body:
Outside endocrinology group
Date of visit: 12/21/2022
Re: Riley Fenton, DOB 11/21/1989

Thank you for moving Ms. Fenton up. She has been fatigued for roughly a year in spite of adequate sleep, and describes coarser, brittle hair, some puffiness around the eyes and constipation. She has had no fever, weight loss or anterior neck pain. Her adrenal replacement is unchanged: hydrocortisone 20 mg in the morning and 10 mg in the afternoon, fludrocortisone 0.1 mg daily. She takes nothing else. No drug allergies.

Family history is notable for type 1 diabetes and Hashimoto disease in her mother, vitiligo in a sister and primary adrenal insufficiency in a maternal aunt. Never smoker, no alcohol. Teaches elementary school.

Exam: pulse 54, BP 110/70, BMI 24. Skin dry and cool. The thyroid is diffusely enlarged and firm, nontender, with no nodules felt. Deep tendon reflexes show a delayed relaxation phase, clearest at the ankle.

Labs today: TSH 18 uIU/mL, free T4 0.4 ng/dL, total T3 60 ng/dL. Anti-thyroglobulin antibody positive. Serum cholesterol elevated, as expected with this degree of hypothyroidism; we will not treat it until she is euthyroid.

Impression: Hashimoto thyroiditis with overt hypothyroidism. Together with her Addison disease this is autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome type 2. Her adrenal replacement was already in place, which is the order we want before thyroid hormone.

Plan: levothyroxine 112 mcg daily, on an empty stomach, apart from food and other pills. Continue current hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone. TSH in 6 to 8 weeks. Given the syndrome, we would screen periodically for other autoimmune conditions; she is aware her family history is relevant.

Allergies: NKDA.
cc: primary care

documents.title: Outside letter reviewed
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Endo letter reviewed. Hashimoto hypothyroidism, APS-2 with her Addison's. Levothyroxine 112 started by endo, added to our list. Endo following TSH.

documents.title: Electronic refill request
documents.author: MA
documents.body:
eRx renewal requests for hydrocortisone 10 mg tabs (#90, 2 qAM + 1 qPM) and fludrocortisone 0.1 mg (#90). Last BMP 12/6 normal. Sent to PCP queue.

PCP: approved x 90 days with 3 refills each.

procedures.procedure: Office visit, established patient, low MDM

documents.title: Follow-up Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Check-in 3 months after starting levothyroxine. Energy a little better. Honest that she forgets the levothyroxine a couple of mornings a week - the hydrocortisone is habit, the new pill isn't, and she takes it with coffee on the way out the door. Endo drew a TSH in February; she doesn't know the number and it isn't in our system.

Exam: vitals as charted. Thyroid still full. Heart regular.

A/P: Hypothyroidism, partly treated, adherence the main issue. Talked through taking it at bedtime or keeping it next to the hydrocortisone, 30-60 min before coffee. Phone alarm set during the visit. BMP for the adrenal side today. Will ask endo for their February labs. Physical in August.

documents.title: Missed appointment
documents.author: front desk
documents.body: No-show for 3:40 follow-up. Texted; she replied that a parent conference ran over and she forgot to call. Not rebooked at her request, will see us at the August physical.

documents.title: Annual Physical
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Annual exam, 33F.

Interval: saw a gynecologist in late June for cycles spacing out to every 2-3 months and a year of trying for a pregnancy. She says they found her thyroid way off again (TSH 12) and a mildly high prolactin they thought came from the thyroid, and asked that we recheck both in about two months. We don't have their letter yet - requested again today. Since then: levothyroxine every night at bedtime, pill organizer next to the hydrocortisone, hasn't missed since. Feels more like herself. Weight up a bit over the spring, holding now.

Adrenal: no sick days this year. Endo visit due fall.

Meds: levothyroxine 112 mcg qHS, hydrocortisone 20/10, fludrocortisone 0.1. NKDA.
Social unchanged. Never smoker, no alcohol.
PHQ-2 0.

Exam: vitals as charted. Skin less dry than in the spring. Thyroid mildly enlarged, smooth. Heart, lungs normal. Abdomen benign. Reflexes normal today. No edema.

A/P
1. Hashimoto hypothyroidism / APS-2 - TSH and prolactin today at gyn's request. CMP for Na/K.
2. Lipids today; endo noted cholesterol was up when she was hypothyroid.
3. Irregular cycles / trying to conceive - per gyn, the plan hinges on the thyroid; they'll take it from here once they see the numbers.
4. HM: Pap 2022 normal. Flu/COVID in October.
Return 6 months.

documents.title: Your physical labs
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Good news: TSH is 3.1 now, in range, and prolactin came back at 14, which is normal - so the gynecologist's hunch that the thyroid was behind it looks right. Cholesterol is normal now that the thyroid is treated. Sodium/potassium, kidney, liver and blood count all normal. I'm faxing these to your gynecologist. Keep doing exactly what you're doing with the bedtime dose.

documents.title: Gynecology consultation
documents.author: gynecology
documents.body:
Outside gynecology practice
Date of service: 06/26/2023
Patient: Riley Fenton, 33 y.o.

Reason for visit: menstrual irregularity and difficulty conceiving.

HPI: Ms. Fenton has APS type 2 with Hashimoto thyroiditis, diagnosed this past winter, and Addison disease. For about six months her periods have come only every two to three months. She and her husband have been trying to conceive for a year without success. She also notes tiredness, some weight gain and feeling cold. She acknowledges she has not been taking her levothyroxine reliably.

Medications: levothyroxine 112 mcg daily (missed often), hydrocortisone 20 mg AM / 10 mg PM, fludrocortisone 0.1 mg daily. Allergies: NKDA.
Family: mother with T1DM and Hashimoto; sister vitiligo; maternal aunt adrenal insufficiency.
Social: teacher; never smoker; no alcohol.

Exam: vitals within normal limits. Weight 67 kg. Skin dry. Reflexes with a slowed relaxation phase.

Labs: TSH 12 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), free T4 0.7 ng/dL (0.9-1.7), prolactin 29 ng/mL (4-23).

Assessment: oligomenorrhea and subfertility in the setting of undertreated primary hypothyroidism. The mild prolactin elevation is most likely secondary to the hypothyroidism.

Plan: daily levothyroxine adherence reviewed at length. Repeat TSH and prolactin in about 8 weeks through her primary care physician. We will reassess cycles and fertility once she is euthyroid; she will call us.

cc: PCP

documents.title: Outside letter reviewed
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Gyn letter from June finally here. Matches what pt told us. Our 8/22 recheck (TSH 3.1, PRL 14) already faxed to them. Filed.

documents.title: Immunization visit
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Flu vaccine L arm, 2023-24 COVID R arm. Tolerated both. Stress-dose reminder given for any fever. Observed 15 min.

procedures.procedure: Office visit, established patient, moderate MDM

documents.title: Office Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
CC: belly pain and bloating, on and off since late spring.

Crampy lower belly pain and bloating, worse after eating, especially big meals. Some days loose stools. No blood, no black stools, no fever, weight steady. No travel, no new meds. Thyroid pills every night, adrenal meds as usual. She wondered about celiac herself because of all the autoimmune things.

Exam: well, vitals as charted. Abdomen soft, not distended, mildly tender low on both sides, no rebound, no guarding, no masses. 

A/P: Postprandial pain and bloating with loose stools in a woman with APS-2 - celiac disease is high on the list. tTG-IgA and total IgA today; she has NOT gone gluten-free yet, and I asked her not to until this is sorted. Will refer to GI if positive.

orders.reason: tTG IgA 86 U/mL with normal total IgA; bloating, postprandial pain

documents.title: Celiac blood test
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Riley - the celiac antibody (tTG-IgA) is positive at 86; anything over 15 is positive, and your total IgA is normal so the test is reliable. This strongly points to celiac disease. The standard next step is an endoscopy with small bowel biopsies by GI, and it only works if you're still eating gluten, so please keep eating normally until then. Referral is in; they should call within the week.

documents.title: RE: Celiac blood test
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Ugh, not surprised. Will keep eating bread for now lol. GI called already, Dec 18.

documents.title: Gastroenterology consultation
documents.author: gastroenterology
documents.body:
Outside gastroenterology group
Visit date: 12/18/2023
Riley Fenton, 34F (DOB 11/21/1989)
Referred for: positive tissue transglutaminase IgA

Ms. Fenton is a 34-year-old with autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome type 2 (Addison disease, Hashimoto hypothyroidism) who comes at the request of her primary care physician. She describes intermittent abdominal pain and bloating that are clearly worse after meals, sometimes with diarrhea. She has seen no blood in the stool and has had no fevers or weight loss. She remains on a normal diet.

PMH: as above; remote iron deficiency anemia treated with oral iron. PSH: none.
Meds: hydrocortisone 20 mg AM / 10 mg PM, fludrocortisone 0.1 mg daily, levothyroxine.
Allergies: no known drug allergies.
Family history: noncontributory to the GI question.
Social: does not smoke or drink.

Exam: abdomen soft and non-distended, with mild tenderness in both lower quadrants; no rebound or guarding. No hepatosplenomegaly.

Data: tTG-IgA 86 U/mL with normal total IgA (11/2023, PCP). Today: hemoglobin 13.2 g/dL, WBC 7,000, platelets 250,000, TSH 2.5, albumin 4.5 g/dL, CRP 2 mg/L.

Assessment: postprandial pain and bloating with a strongly positive tTG in a patient with polyglandular autoimmunity. Celiac disease is likely. Normal albumin, hemoglobin and CRP are reassuring against a more serious inflammatory process, which was her main worry.

Plan: upper endoscopy with duodenal biopsies, scheduled 1/9. Continue a gluten-containing diet until then. If confirmed, strict gluten-free diet and dietitian referral.

cc: PCP

reports.text: Specimen A: duodenal bulb, biopsies x2. Specimen B: second portion of duodenum, biopsies x4. Microscopic: small bowel mucosa with partial villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes (greater than 40 per 100 enterocytes). No granulomas, no dysplasia, no organisms.
reports.conclusion: Duodenum, biopsies: partial villous atrophy with intraepithelial lymphocytosis, Marsh 3a, consistent with celiac disease in the setting of positive serology.

documents.title: Upper endoscopy report
documents.author: gastroenterology
documents.body:
Procedure: esophagogastroduodenoscopy with biopsy, 01/09/2024, outside endoscopy unit.
Indication: positive tTG-IgA, postprandial bloating.
Sedation: monitored anesthesia care. Hydrocortisone dose doubled the morning of the procedure per her endocrinologist.
Findings: normal esophagus. Normal stomach. Duodenal bulb and second portion grossly unremarkable. Biopsies taken from bulb and D2.
Complications: none.
Pathology (01/12): Marsh 3a changes, consistent with celiac disease.
Recommendations: strict lifelong gluten-free diet; referral to our dietitian placed; repeat tTG in 6 to 12 months to confirm adherence.
Allergies: NKDA.
cc: PCP

documents.title: Outside records reviewed
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: EGD + path reviewed: celiac confirmed, Marsh 3a. Added to problem list. GI arranging dietitian. Iron and vitamin D at next visit.

documents.title: Gluten question
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Hi, so it's official, celiac. Quick question - do I need to worry about gluten in my hydrocortisone or thyroid pills? The dietitian said to ask my pharmacy and my doctor.

documents.title: RE: Gluten question
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Good question. The generic hydrocortisone, fludrocortisone and levothyroxine you're on are gluten-free per the manufacturers' statements your pharmacy pulled for me. If the pharmacy ever switches the maker, ask them to check again. Let's see you in February to go over how the diet is going and check iron and vitamin D.

procedures.procedure: Office visit, established patient, low MDM

documents.title: Follow-up Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Six weeks gluten-free after the EGD. Bloating noticeably less, stools more formed. Had one accidental exposure at a staff lunch, sore and crampy for a day. Dietitian visit done, husband doing the shopping with her. Thyroid and adrenal meds unchanged and taken.

Exam: vitals as charted, weight stable. Abdomen soft, nontender today.

A/P
- Celiac disease: early response to diet. Iron studies, vitamin D, CBC today given the past iron deficiency. GI to recheck tTG later this year; I'll add it to her physical if they haven't.
- APS-2: hypothyroid and adrenal stable.
Physical in August.

documents.title: Iron and vitamin D
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Iron stores, vitamin D and your blood count are all normal - nothing to add. Keep up the diet.

procedures.procedure: Telehealth visit, established patient, low MDM

orders.reason: Depigmented patches hands and face; sister with vitiligo

documents.title: Video Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Video from her classroom after dismissal, identity verified.

Noticed pale patches on the backs of both hands and one near her right temple over the winter, getting a little bigger. They don't itch or hurt. Her sister has vitiligo and she thinks this looks the same.

On camera: several well-defined paler patches on dorsal hands and right temple, no redness or scale visible. Limited by video.

A/P: Depigmented patches, likely vitiligo given her autoimmune history and family history. Dermatology referral for confirmation and treatment options. Sunscreen on the patches meanwhile.

medications.sig: Apply a thin layer to the white patches on face and hands twice daily

documents.title: Dermatology consultation
documents.author: dermatology
documents.body:
Outside dermatology office - new patient consultation, 6/17/2024

Riley Fenton, age 34. Referred by her PCP for white patches.

She has autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome type 2 (Addison disease, Hashimoto hypothyroidism) and celiac disease diagnosed this January. Over the past several months she has developed white spots that are slowly enlarging; they cause no symptoms. Sister has vitiligo.

Medications: hydrocortisone, fludrocortisone, levothyroxine. NKDA.

Examination: multiple flat depigmented macules with sharp, well-defined borders on the dorsal hands and the face (right temple). No scale, no erythema, no atrophy. Wood's lamp makes the patches stand out sharply from the surrounding skin.

Labs today: TSH 3.5, fasting glucose 88, ANA negative, CBC within normal limits.

Impression: nonsegmental vitiligo.

Plan: tacrolimus 0.1% ointment twice daily to facial and hand patches. Broad-spectrum sunscreen. Discussed phototherapy as a later option if response is slow. Return in 6 months or as needed.

Allergies: NKDA. cc: PCP

documents.title: Outside letter reviewed
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Derm: vitiligo confirmed; tacrolimus ointment started by derm. Lists updated.

documents.title: Annual Physical
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Yearly exam before school starts. 34F.

Year in review: celiac confirmed in January, strict GF since, GI symptoms basically gone. Vitiligo diagnosed in June, using tacrolimus on face and hands, too early to tell. Levothyroxine nightly, hydrocortisone/fludrocortisone unchanged. No adrenal sick days.

Meds: levothyroxine 112 mcg qHS, hydrocortisone 20 mg AM/10 mg PM, fludrocortisone 0.1 mg, tacrolimus 0.1% oint BID. NKDA.
Never smoker, no alcohol. PHQ-2: 1.

Exam: vitals as charted. Depigmented macules dorsal hands and right temple. Thyroid mildly enlarged, smooth. Cardiopulmonary normal. Abdomen soft, nontender. Joints without swelling. No edema.

A/P
1. Celiac disease - tTG today to check the diet.
2. APS-2 / hypothyroidism / Addison's - CMP today; endo has her TSH.
3. Vitiligo - per derm.
4. HM: Pap current to 2027. Flu/COVID in October.

documents.title: Celiac antibody
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Your celiac antibody is down to 11 from 86 last fall - under the cutoff of 15, which tells us the gluten-free diet is working. Electrolytes, kidney, liver and blood count are normal. Have a good start to the year.

documents.title: Immunization visit
documents.author: MA
documents.body: 2024-25 flu (L) and COVID (R) given, lot numbers in the MAR. No issues after 15 minutes. Reminded about extra hydrocortisone if feverish.

procedures.procedure: Office visit, established patient, moderate MDM

orders.reason: Symmetric small-joint hand and knee pain with morning stiffness and swelling

documents.title: Office Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
S: Since around June her hands and both knees ache, worst in the morning - takes her a good while to be able to make a fist, and holding a dry-erase marker is hard first period. Eases by lunchtime. Tired again. No rash, no fever, no recent illness or injury. Thyroid and adrenal routine unchanged, still GF.

O: Vitals as charted. Puffy, tender knuckles and middle finger joints on both hands. Knees without effusion, nontender.

A/P: Symmetric inflammatory-sounding small-joint arthritis with morning stiffness, several months - needs rheumatology. Referral placed, asked for the next opening. She'd rather they draw the inflammatory labs so she isn't stuck twice. Acetaminophen as needed meanwhile; avoids NSAIDs on her own.

documents.title: Pharmacy call
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Pharmacist called: new rx for methotrexate 2.5 mg, 6 tabs once weekly, and folic acid 1 mg daily from an outside rheumatologist, first filled 1/2. Their interaction check flagged it against her chart and they wanted to confirm we're aware. We had no rheum note on file. Told them PCP would review. Message sent to patient.

documents.title: Rheumatology visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Hi Riley - your pharmacy let us know about the methotrexate. We haven't gotten the rheumatologist's note yet. Can you tell me what they found and the plan? I'll ask them to send it.

medications.sig: Take 6 tablets (15 mg) by mouth once a week on the same day

documents.title: RE: Rheumatology visit
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Sorry, should've told you! Saw rheum on New Year's Eve. They said rheumatoid arthritis, both blood tests for it positive and inflammation up. Methotrexate 6 pills every Sunday plus folic acid every day. They did a pregnancy test and hepatitis tests first and talked to me about not getting pregnant on it - we're not trying right now anyway. Labs every few months, they said you can draw them.

documents.title: List update
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: RA added per patient report; methotrexate 15 mg weekly and folic acid 1 mg added (outside rx). Records request faxed to rheumatology. Will draw CBC/CMP q3mo per their plan once the order arrives.

documents.title: Rheumatology consultation
documents.author: rheumatology
documents.body:
Outside rheumatology practice
Date of service: 12/31/2024
Patient: Riley Fenton (DOB 11/21/1989)

History: 35-year-old teacher with APS type 2 (Addison disease, Hashimoto hypothyroidism), celiac disease and vitiligo seen earlier this year, referred for joint pain. For six months she has had fatigue and pain in the hands and knees, symmetric, with stiffness each morning. No recent infection or trauma.

Medications: hydrocortisone 20 mg AM and 10 mg PM, fludrocortisone 0.1 mg daily, tacrolimus ointment. NKDA.
Family: mother T1DM and Hashimoto; sister vitiligo; maternal aunt adrenal insufficiency.
Social: never smoker, no alcohol.

Exam: synovitis with swelling and tenderness of the MCP and PIP joints of both hands. Knees without effusion. No rheumatoid nodules. Skin with vitiligo of hands and face.

Labs: Hgb 12.1, ESR 45 mm/hr, CRP 24 mg/L, RF positive, anti-CCP positive, TSH 2.5. Hepatitis B surface antigen negative, hepatitis C antibody negative. Urine hCG negative.

Assessment: seropositive rheumatoid arthritis, active.

Plan: methotrexate 15 mg orally once weekly with folic acid 1 mg daily. Not attempting pregnancy at present; counseled that methotrexate is teratogenic and must be stopped at least 3 months before trying, and that reliable contraception is needed while on it - she and her husband will use contraception. Avoid alcohol (she does not drink). CBC with differential and CMP every 4 weeks for 3 months, then every 3 months; PCP office may draw. Return in 3 months.

cc: primary care

documents.title: Outside letter reviewed
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Rheum letter (12/31) arrived today, about 8 weeks late. Consistent with what she told us. Standing CBC/CMP order entered for q3mo; first monthly draws were done at rheum's lab per patient.

documents.title: Methotrexate monitoring
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: CBC and CMP normal, liver enzymes normal on methotrexate. Copy to rheumatology. Portal note sent.

procedures.procedure: Office visit, established patient, moderate MDM

documents.title: Follow-up Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Five months on methotrexate. Mornings much easier, she can grip again. Energy improved. Still GF, tTG was normal last summer. Adrenal fine, no sick days this winter.

Meds: levothyroxine 112 mcg, hydrocortisone 20/10, fludrocortisone 0.1, methotrexate 15 mg weekly, folic acid 1 mg, tacrolimus oint. NKDA.

Exam: vitals as charted. No synovitis in the hands today. Thyroid smooth, mildly full. Heart regular. Skin: depigmented macules hands and right temple.

A/P
1. RA - better on MTX. CBC/CMP today for monitoring.
2. Hypothyroidism - TSH/free T4 today (endo visit delayed to fall on their end).
3. Addison's - BMP portion of CMP.
4. Celiac, vitiligo - stable.
Physical in August; discuss pneumonia and shingles vaccines then since she's on methotrexate.

documents.title: Lab results
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: All normal: thyroid (TSH 1.9, free T4 1.2), blood counts and liver tests on the methotrexate, sodium and potassium. Enjoy the end of the school year.

documents.title: Hair coming out
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Weird one. For about a week I'm finding clumps of hair on my pillow and my husband found a totally bald round spot on the back of my head, and now I see another one. Doesn't hurt or itch. Is this the methotrexate?? My dermatologist can see me the 30th, should I go to that?

documents.title: RE: Hair coming out
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Methotrexate can thin hair a little all over, but round, completely bald patches sound more like alopecia areata, another autoimmune condition that travels with the ones you have. Your dermatologist is the right person and the 30th is fine. If you notice a rash, sores, or the patches becoming red or scaly before then, let me know and I'll see you.

documents.title: Dermatology follow-up
documents.author: dermatology
documents.body:
Outside dermatology office - follow-up visit 6/30/2025

Riley Fenton, 35. Known to us for vitiligo. Three weeks of hair shedding: handfuls on the pillow in the mornings and several round areas of complete hair loss on the scalp. No pain, itch or burning. Thyroid tests from her PCP last month were normal.

Meds: hydrocortisone, fludrocortisone, levothyroxine, methotrexate 15 mg weekly with folic acid, tacrolimus ointment. NKDA.

Exam: three sharply circumscribed round patches of alopecia on the scalp, smooth skin, no erythema, scale or scarring. No lymphadenopathy. Nails: no pitting or onycholysis. Known vitiligo macules on hands and face, stable; the rest of the skin is unremarkable.

Impression: alopecia areata, patchy.

Procedure: after verbal consent, intralesional triamcinolone acetonide 10 mg/mL was injected into the three patches, about 0.1 mL per site, total 1.2 mL. Tolerated well.

Plan: repeat injections every 4 to 6 weeks as needed. Continue tacrolimus to vitiligo. Return 6 weeks.

Regional hospital - Discharge Summary
Admitted: 12/24/2025 via the emergency department. Discharged: 12/29/2025.
Patient: Riley Fenton, 36F

Principal diagnosis: thyroid storm due to Graves disease.
Secondary: atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response, resolved; autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome type 2 with primary adrenal insufficiency; rheumatoid arthritis; celiac disease; vitiligo; alopecia areata.

Presentation: two days of palpitations, breathlessness and fever. She had been without methimazole for about a week; she continued her hydrocortisone. In the ED: T 39.8 C, HR 132, BP 155/95, RR 28. Agitated and intermittently confused. Skin warm and moist, fine tremor, enlarged nontender thyroid with an audible bruit. ECG: atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response.

Labs: total T3 260 ng/dL, total T4 18 ug/dL, TSH <0.01, WBC 16,000. Electrolytes and creatinine normal. Urinalysis negative. Blood cultures no growth. Portable chest film clear.

Course: admitted to the ICU. Treated with propranolol, propylthiouracil, potassium iodide given an hour after the first PTU dose, IV fluids, cooling and stress-dose IV hydrocortisone, which also covered her adrenal insufficiency. Converted to sinus rhythm on hospital day 2 with rate control. Given a CHA2DS2-VASc score of 1, anticoagulation was not started. Mental status cleared by day 2. Transferred to the floor on 12/26; switched back to methimazole and oral hydrocortisone, tapered to her usual dose by discharge.

Discharge medications: methimazole 20 mg twice daily; propranolol 20 mg three times daily; hydrocortisone 20 mg AM / 10 mg PM; fludrocortisone 0.1 mg daily; methotrexate 15 mg weekly; folic acid 1 mg daily; tacrolimus 0.1% ointment; levothyroxine 112 mcg daily (home list).

Allergies: NKDA.

Regional hospital - Discharge Summary
Admission: 07/01/2026 (via ED). Discharge: 07/06/2026.
Patient: Riley Fenton, 36F. Allergies: NKDA.

Diagnoses: adrenal crisis in known primary adrenal insufficiency (APS type 2); symptomatic cholelithiasis, status post laparoscopic cholecystectomy 07/03/2026.
Other: Graves disease s/p total thyroidectomy 01/2026, on levothyroxine; rheumatoid arthritis; celiac disease; vitiligo; alopecia areata.

History: she was scheduled for elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy on the morning of 7/1. She presented to the ED instead with severe abdominal pain and vomiting; for two days she had been unable to keep down her medicines, including hydrocortisone.

ED: BP 85/50, HR 120, T 38.5 C. Abdomen diffusely tender, no rebound or guarding. Sodium 130, potassium 5.5, glucose 55 mg/dL, 8 AM cortisol 3 ug/dL drawn before steroid. Liver tests and lipase normal. Blood pressure remained low after 2 L of normal saline.

Course: hydrocortisone 100 mg IV given, IV dextrose for the low glucose, and further saline. Blood pressure, glucose and mental status recovered within hours. Admitted on hydrocortisone 50 mg IV every 6 hours. The operation was postponed. Sodium and potassium normalized by the next morning. Laparoscopic cholecystectomy performed 07/03 under stress-dose coverage without complication. Pathology: cholelithiasis, benign. Hydrocortisone tapered to her home dose by 07/05. Tolerating diet at discharge.

Discharge medications: hydrocortisone 20 mg every morning and 10 mg every evening; fludrocortisone 0.1 mg daily; levothyroxine 112 mcg daily; methotrexate 15 mg weekly (resume after one missed week); folic acid 1 mg daily; tacrolimus 0.1% ointment. NEW: hydrocortisone 100 mg injection kit for emergency use.

Patient education: sick-day rules given in writing - double or triple oral hydrocortisone for fever or illness; if vomiting or unable to take tablets, inject 100 mg IM and come to the ED. Medical alert identification advised.

Follow-up: PCP 2-4 weeks; surgery clinic 2 weeks; endocrinology.

documents.body: Hi! Teachers go back next week. Our school nurse wants a letter from you saying what to do if I get sick at school and that she can give me the hydrocortisone shot. Could you write one? Thank you.

documents.title: Letter for school health office
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
To the school nurse:

Ms. Riley Fenton is my patient. She has primary adrenal insufficiency and takes daily hydrocortisone. In an emergency her body cannot make the stress hormone it needs.

If she is vomiting and cannot keep down her tablets, has a severe illness or injury, or appears confused, faint or very weak, she or you should give her emergency hydrocortisone 100 mg by intramuscular injection in the outer thigh (she carries the kit) and call 911. Tell the responders she has adrenal insufficiency and has received hydrocortisone.

She has my permission to keep the kit with her at school. Please call our office with any questions.

Primary care physician
